work.title: Shenoute: Seeks

paragraphs.text: They will destroy Nineveh. We saw no sign through him, and we turned away from our ways.
But God came to you. He performed mighty deeds that neither Jonah nor Solomon nor anyone else [?] among you, and you did not repent.
This rebuke that will come upon us comes from people who had despaired of their lives for a time and did not think they would see anything good.

Yet they did see it, and the Lord added this concerning them: they will rise on the day of judgment and condemn this generation. What, then, will we do when faced with the rebuke of these multitudes of saints,

who proclaimed to us the ways of life and the deeds of salvation, and who themselves gave their blood for us, just like God, who gave his own for us—Jesus, to whom all judgment belongs, [?] the mouth of those who were promised that they would accuse us? He is the one who will command those to whom he promised that they would sit on thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and judge all human beings who have lived on earth, and judge angels. What will they judge them for?
They will judge them,
saying, “Instead of helping others escape Satan’s power and every evil,
you yourselves rushed all the more toward evil, like birds swooping down on a carcass.
When you lusted after the daughters of human beings, you committed evil with them.
You stirred up war on earth instead of peace.”
And they will also pass judgment on us.
What will they condemn us for?
“You did not obey our words. You did not strive to imitate our deeds. You did not desire our ways.”
I will say no more than this.
It is enough for them to say this alone, all together, from the patriarch to the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints, rebuking our shamelessness:
“God came to you.
God was crucified for you.
You were not willing to turn away from the deeds of the demons.”
It was with one voice that a crowd of people, who had prepared themselves for murder, shouted at the Place of the Skull,
“Take him away! Take him away! Crucify him!”
Likewise, a single voice will come from his holy judgment seat,
“Take them away! Take them away!
“Take away the chaff and the weeds!
Take away the bad fish and the goats!
Bind their hands and feet and throw them into Hades!
Punish them! Punish them in that place!”

If those whom blind Belial had blinded cried out together, “Do not release this man,” and their voices prevailed, then how could they fail to cry out together—the thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of archangels, and the entire multitude of his chosen ones—“Do not release these people from their eternal punishment!”
And how much more will their voices prevail!
“Do not have mercy on these people who do not believe in you.”
“Do not have compassion on those who did not recognize you as God and the Son of God.”
But how did they arrest him?
Was it with hostility, rushing at him in all their anger with their swords and clubs, dragging him before a governor like a robber?
Or did they lead him along, inviting him with gentleness and peace, to take him to a dinner?
And how will those who die without believing in him find relief?

Or where will they escape the furious wrath of all his angels, who will begin from the four corners throughout the whole earth on the day when he sends them to gather all the nations before his judgment seat?
Certainly, they also took him out to destroy him with savage cruelty.
Sobriety or gentleness cannot arise from wickedness or envy.
How, then, will they hold back from destroying the soul and body of those who deny that Jesus is the Christ,

who endured patiently on the cross while they said these wicked things against him, opening their mouths against him and raising their voices against him like lions and calves, with laughter and loud shouting,
so that we might now hear the words of the Gospels read to us in a voice of peace, humility, and gentleness?
Though they did all these things to him, he was not disturbed.
But they were not merely agitated;
they were also falling backward, striking their backs against the ground.
And they were fighting, threatening, and striking him.
But he was not revealing his divinity in its fullness, so that he would not destroy the earth in his anger from that very day because of those who were doing evil to him.
How would his kingdom become still more filled with good and righteous people and sinless multitudes, and sinners who had all repented through the preaching of the gospel?

But amid the hostility and hatred that the scribes, Pharisees, chief priests, elders, and all those people directed against him, the love and all the peace of his church and all his congregations increased.
And he will further increase his peace upon us, adding still more of his love toward us, and we too toward one another.

Anyone who does not take these words to heart so as to renounce the devil and keep sin away from his soul, lest he destroy it like a male pig and pasture it like a male donkey, does not know that wisdom has an advantage over foolishness, just as light has an advantage over darkness, as Ecclesiastes said.
Whoever does not accept these words does not understand that what the eyes see is better than wandering with one's soul.
Nor does he understand that the light is sweet: it is good for our eyes to see Christ.
And again, that there is an advantage for those who see the sun, which is he himself—Jesus, the sun of righteousness.
For if there were no heavenly desire greater than every desire in the world, perhaps some fool would say that those who do the deeds of the flesh are not impoverished.
Listen and see what the one whose hope is in the Lord said,
so that you will not abandon the will of Jesus, your Lord and your God, for the will of human beings,
and so that you will not abandon purity or virginity for a desire for marriage, not knowing that you will have your fill of it,
and so that you will not abandon the desire for spiritual deeds for excessive bodily deeds.
He therefore said, “My soul refused to be comforted.
I remembered God and rejoiced.”
You, however, rejoice in doing deeds that should cause you grief, and you comfort yourself with people who are hostile to God and his laws.
But we read: “I did not sit in their assembly while they were laughing.”
And: “I did not sit with a worthless assembly.”
“I hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly.”
Yet we sit down with them, love them, and become their companions.
Here is comfort that is truly empty!
Here is a friendship that makes a person an enemy of Jesus: this is our desire to find comfort through pagan people.
If we are going to make friends for ourselves, let us choose them from among God's people, and let us comfort one another with the comfort of which the saints spoke:
“So that we may comfort one another through the faith we share, ours and theirs.”
Will not the fainthearted among us say, “How much talking there has been from yesterday until today!”
Or, “How long will he go on?”
Why, instead, have we not said, “We have spent a long time in our acts of violence, our defilements, and all our sins”?
And, “All that filth that has clung to us has scarcely been washed away at all, even after all these words, like abundant water, to wash it off and remove it from us.”
Then we too may say, “My soul will boast in the Lord.
Let the humble hear and rejoice.
Exalt the Lord with me, and exalt his name together.”
Look, I will stop now.
So I beg anyone who has not sinned to continue to guard himself.

And I ask anyone who is enticed by it to flee from it, as someone being set free from it through these words. And I ask anyone who has resolved in his heart not to sin after hearing these words not to do it again.
And if we all resolve in our hearts not to sin from the day we heard these words, we believe—and we will not doubt—that Jesus will forgive us for everything we have done.
